paras.text: In this section, we compare the contributions of DLT and CLT in predicting variance in reading times, using naturalistic reading data based on a Japanese corpus. Testing both theories with a head-final language like Japanese is important since their predictions diverge drastically in head-final languages, as described above. The code for the calculation of the predictors and for the statistical analysis reported below is available at https://osf.io/62utg/.

The BCCWJ corpus is available at https://clrd.ninjal.ac.jp/bccwj/en/index.html (license required). The UD annotation of the corpus is available at https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/ja_bccwj/index.html. The BCCWJ-SPR2 dataset is available at https://github.com/masayu-a/BCCWJ-SPR2.
https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/ja_bccwjluw/.

Understanding a written or spoken sentence requires reconstruction of the structured meaning from the linear sequence of words that is perceived. How this is achieved is a central question in the study of human sentence comprehension. Many theories of comprehension have assumed that it involves encoding and retrieval of information using working memory (Demberg et al., 2013; Gibson, 2000; Isono, 2024; Lewis & Vasishth, 2005; McElree, 2000). These theories point to various factors that can tax working memory and make sentences difficult to comprehend.

One possible structural factor is distance, or locality. A widely-held assumption in linguistics and cognitive science more generally is that information encoded in working memory degrades gradually. This is either because of time-based decay, interference with subsequent information, or both (Anderson et al., 2004; Lewis & Vasishth, 2005; Oberauer et al., 2012; Ricker et al., 2016; Van Dyke & McElree, 2011). As representations degrade, they become harder to retrieve and integrate with later information. Applied to sentence comprehension, this view predicts that linguistic elements that are related to each other but linearly distant in presentation will be difficult to process. This processing difficulty is called a locality effect.

A simple and popular approach to predict locality effects is to use a dependency grammar, as proposed by Dependency Locality Theory (DLT) (Gibson, 1998, 2000; see also Futrell, Gibson, & Levy, 2020). In (1), for example, reporter has to be retrieved from working memory when disliked is encountered downstream to establish the subject-verb relation between them. Since this dependency is longer in (1b) than in (1a), DLT predicts that disliked is more difficult to process in (1b). The difficulty is expected to be observed as an increase in the time spent on the word in spontaneous reading, for example.(1) a. The reporter who the senator attacked disliked the editor. b. The reporter who the senator who John met attacked disliked the editor.

Evidence for such locality effects, however, has been mixed. Robust effects have been found in certain constructions such as English relative clauses (Bartek et al., 2011; Grodner & Gibson, 2005; Roland et al., 2021; Staub, 2010), but are absent in others such as verb-final structures of German and Japanese (Levy & Keller, 2013; Nakatani & Gibson, 2010). The effect is also missing in large-scale reading time data based on naturalistic corpora in English (Demberg & Keller, 2008; Demberg et al., 2013; Dotlačil, 2021). This instability of locality effects contrasts with expectation-based effects (Hale, 2001; Levy, 2008) (i.e., less expected input is more difficult), which have gained much empirical support across languages and constructions (e.g., Wilcox et al., 2023).

Addressing these problems, Isono (2024) recently proposed a new theory of locality effect based on Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) (Steedman, 1996, 2000), dubbed Category Locality Theory (CLT). According to this work, earlier theories of locality effect faced empirical problems not because locality is an insignificant factor in human sentence comprehension but because of the way the distance is measured. Isono argued that syntactic distance measured in terms of CCG rather than dependencies explains the seemingly puzzling previous results, specifically the processing difficulty in English relative clauses and the lack of difficulty in verb-final structures. Furthermore, the study demonstrated that the CCG-based distance predicts reading times for an English naturalistic corpus (Natural Stories corpus, Futrell et al. (2021)), even when expectation-based predictors are controlled for. These results suggest that CCG reflects some important aspects of the syntactic representation used by the human parser.

With this background, this study further tests the prediction of CLT and compares it with that of DLT using naturalistic texts in Japanese. More precisely, we ask the following questions:Do DLT and CLT explain variance in reading times in Japanese naturalistic reading?If both do, which explains more? Does one explain variance that the other does not?The language is typologically different from English as it is strictly head-final, and is notorious for not following the dependency-based prediction of locality effects (Nakatani, 2021; Nakatani & Gibson, 2010). While Isono (2024) claims that CLT accounts for the lack of the locality effect at clause-final verbs, whether CLT predicts reading times in verb-final languages in a broad-coverage manner has not been investigated empirically. To anticipate the results, our results favor CLT over DLT.

This subsection introduces Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) (Ades & Steedman, 1982; Steedman, 1996, 2000), which is the basis of the theory tested in this study, CLT. A key characteristic of CCG is that the structure-building mechanism for the competence-level derivation can also be used to model incremental performance. CLT is concerned with the cost of those structure-building operations. We therefore begin by introducing CCG as a competence grammar and then describe how they are used to model performance.

CCG (Steedman, 1996, 2000) belongs to a family of grammar formalisms called categorial grammars (Ajdukiewicz, 1935/1967; Bar-Hillel, 1953; Kubota & Levine, 2020; Lambek, 1958, 1961; Moortgat, 1997; Morrill, 1994, i.a.). In categorial grammars, including CCG, each linguistic expression is associated with a category that specifies its syntactic behavior. The set of categories is defined inductively as follows:(2) a. There is a finite set of primitive categories: S, NP, N, …. b. If X and Y are (primitive or functional) categories, X/Y and X\Y are functional categories.1The basic behavior of functional categories is specified by the application rules, defined below.(3) X and Y stand for an arbitrary category. In each rule, the categories above the line are the input categories (or premises), and the one below the line is the output category (or conclusion); beside the line is the symbol for the rule. The following is an example of a simple derivation using just these rules:(4) This system resembles feature-based implementations of Merge in Minimalist syntax (Adger, 2003; Chomsky, 1995; Stabler, 2012). Like uninterpretable features in Minimalism, argument categories (/Y or \Y) specify the features of the expression it combines with, and are consumed once such a combination is made. Categorial grammars differ from Minimalism in that they allow complex categories to be targeted as an argument. For example, the following analysis of a relative clause assumes that the relative pronoun selects a complex category S\NP, effectively binding the missing subject:(5) Categorial grammar just with the application rules, called AB grammar after Ajdukiewicz (1935/1967) and Bar-Hillel (1953), is not expressive enough to analyze natural languages. Various extensions have been proposed to overcome its limitations (de Groote, 2001; Kubota & Levine, 2020; Lambek, 1958, 1961; Moortgat, 1997; Morrill, 1994; Morrill et al., 2011; Muskens, 2003, i.a.). CCG is one of such extensions, and characteristically uses combinatory rules, which are associated with combinators from the combinatory logic (Curry & Feys, 1958). While the exact set of combinatory rules available is debatable (Hoyt & Baldridge, 2008), the most important ones are the (harmonic, first-order) composition rules (B) and type-raising rules (T)2, defined below:(6) Here, T stands for a variable category. When there are multiple variable categories in the same derivation, they will be distinguished by an index (T1, T2, …). As the name suggests, composition rules compose two functional categories into a new functional category. Type-raising rules modify an argument category to a functional category. The following analysis of an object-extracted relative clause uses these rules:(7) Note that in this analysis, the string John attacked is analyzed as having the category S/NP. This is an appropriate characterization of the string, since it would be a full sentence if it is followed by an object NP. As can be seen from this example, the combination of composition and type-raising is powerful enough to model basic displacement phenomena.

In (7), the category S/NP assigned to John attacked is understood as describing the string as a gapped clause. Another interpretation of the same category is that it describes the state of the parser that has processed John attacked and awaits an incoming NP. Thus, the combinatory rules in CCG, used to account for competence-level data such as relative clauses, can also be used to model incremental processing. The incremental processing of a sentence, say John attacked Bill, can be illustrated as a derivation, as shown below.(8) This derivation is said to be incremental because it integrates each word from left to right into a single constituent. This contrasts with the normal form tree (Eisner, 1996), which makes the least use of composition:(9)

In CCG (and in categorial grammars in general), there is a transparent mapping between syntax and semantics via the Curry-Howard correspondence. Having a syntactic analysis for a fragment therefore guarantees that there is a logical form reflecting the syntactic structure. In the current case, the S/NP category for John attacked is associated with the term λx.attacked(x)(John), appropriately expressing that John is the agent of the attacking action and the patient term is waited for (for details about compositional semantics in CCG, see Steedman, 2000, 2019). This accounts for the well-known fact that human incremental sentence processing has immediate access to the semantics of the fragments as well as their syntax (Kamide et al., 2003; Tanenhaus et al., 1995).

Since CCG is compatible with incremental parsing, several studies have used it to model behavioral and neural data during language processing (Kajikawa et al., 2024; Ozaki et al., 2024; Stanojević et al., 2023). While these studies use the number of rule applications as the predictor, Category Locality Theory (CLT) (Isono, 2024) proposed to use CCG to model memory constraints. The key feature of CCG that is important for CLT is that it does not provide a fully incremental parse for every sentence (Demberg, 2012). One of the structures that cannot be parsed fully incrementally with the canonical rules mentioned above is the object relative clause. (10) is the parse that is as incremental as possible:(10) Here the embedded subject the senator is not combined directly with the preceding the reporter who because there is no applicable rule that leads to an appropriate parse:(11) Therefore, at the time the senator is processed, the parser has to maintain two separate categories/constituents. The core idea of CLT is that having separate CCG constituents as in the current example taxes working memory. The original paper discusses two ways in which working memory is taxed. In the current paper we will refer to these ways as integration cost and storage cost respectively, following the terminology of DLT (Gibson, 2000).

The integration cost models the locality effect, and is incurred when an old constituent is retrieved from memory for integration with a newer constituent. The cost should be larger when the distance between the point of the formation of the constituent and the point of its retrieval is longer. This prediction is derived from two widely-held assumptions in psycholinguistics (Demberg et al., 2013; Gibson, 2000; Lewis & Vasishth, 2005; McElree, 2000). First, the activation of a linguistic representation held in working memory degrades over time, through time-based decay, interference, or both. Second, the latency of the retrieval of a representation is dependent on its activation. The exact forms of the activation decay and the activation–retrieval latency relation are not part of the core claim of CLT; Isono (2024) distinguishes those as “auxiliary assumptions” to implement CLT. In this paper we will empirically test several possible measures of distance.

In the current relative clause example, an integration cost is predicted at attacked, where the reporter who is retrieved for integration with the senator attacked. The cost is determined by the length of the intervening material, the senator in this case. Isono (2024) argues that CLT integration cost accounts for the well-known processing difficulty of English object-relative clauses (Bartek et al., 2011; Grodner & Gibson, 2005; King & Just, 1991; Roland et al., 2021; Staub, 2010). Isono also shows that it is a significant predictor of reading times for English texts in the Natural Stories corpus (Futrell et al., 2021). DLT integration cost (Gibson, 2000; Shain et al., 2016), in contrast, showed no significant effect for the same dataset.

Isono (2024) also considers the storage cost of CCG-based parsing. This idea is borrowed from DLT (Gibson, 2000). DLT assumes that the storage of the structure built so far can slow down processing of new materials since the two processes use the same pool of cognitive resources. The storage cost is quantified by the number of syntactic heads required to complete the sentence. Controlled experiments in English and Spanish support the presence of DLT storage cost (Chen et al., 2005; Ristic et al., 2022). In CCG-based parsing, the storage cost should be contingent on the number of separate constituents, which have to be held in working memory for later integration. In the current case, the storage of the reporter who should slow down the processing of the senator. Isono (2024) shows that CCG-based storage cost is also a significant predictor of reading times for the Natural Stories corpus. Though the original work does not include CCG-based storage cost in CLT proper (the integration cost was the only component of CLT), this paper will refer to it as CLT storage cost because we then have a nice correspondence between the integration/storage costs in CLT and DLT.

When integration and storage costs arise during the processing of a sentence depends on when CCG fails to provide a fully incremental parse, and when it fails to depends on the set of rules available. In the current discussion we assume most basic rules of application (>, <), first-order harmonic composition (B), and type-raising (T). But there are other rules discussed in the literature, and they can affect psycholinguistic predictions. For example, adding a rule known as the >D rule (Hoyt & Baldridge, 2008) makes the derivation of a English object relative clause (10) more incremental (Demberg, 2012), enabling the integration of the reporter who and the senator without attacked. This would shift the locus of the integration cost to senator. An extreme case would be a complete set of combinatory rules that can analyze any left fragment of a grammatical expression as a single constituent. A parser with such a complete set of rules would achieve fully incremental parsing based on powerful prediction, and CLT predicts no locality effects at all. The previous result by Isono (2024) suggests that this is not the case, since reading times for an English corpus could be modeled by a less effortful CCG parser. In fact, reading times for the Natural Stories corpus were better predicted without the >D rule. In the corpus analysis of this study, we will also consider different rule sets.

Figure 1 illustrates the predictions of CLT and DLT for the same object relative clause.3 In the figure, arcs above the text represent dependencies. Non-local dependencies, indicated by blue arcs, should incur processing costs: a storage cost is predicted in areas covered by the arc, and an integration cost proportional to the length of the arc is predicted at the right end of the arc. Below the text is the graph for CCG-based processing. Here, each node represents the category that the parser assigned to the string that has been observed so far. The edges indicate how these categories are integrated to yield new categories for larger constituents. Here we illustrate CCG parsing as a system of state transition with multiple states held in parallel when necessary, as in Wanner and Maratsos (1978). When an integration is non-local, as indicated by a red edge, storage and integration costs are predicted. Again, the storage cost should affect the processing of the area covered by the edge, and the integration cost should be incurred at the right end of the edge. As can be seen from the figure, both CLT and DLT predict a non-zero integration cost (i.e., a locality effect) at the embedded verb, and a non-zero storage cost over the embedded subject. These predictions match previous experimental observations, but the two theories posit different sources of the observed locality effect: in DLT, it is the length of the dependencies; in CLT, it is the complexity of the logical/grammatical structure, which prevents fully incremental integration.

While DLT and CLT make similar predictions regarding English relative clauses, which is important given that the locality effect in this construction is robust, they make different predictions in other constructions. For example, DLT predicts locality effects in English matrix subject-verb dependencies, but CLT does not (controlled experiments on this point show mixed results (Bartek et al., 2011; Grodner & Gibson, 2005)). Another notable example is the verb-final structure, which will be discussed below. As Isono (2024) notes, however, DLT and CLT are not necessarily mutually exclusive accounts of processing cost. Both theories may contribute to the prediction of reading times if different components of our linguistic faculty, such as semantics and syntax, employ dependency- and CCG-like representations, respectively. From this consideration, in our corpus analysis, we test statistical models that include DLT and CLT simultaneously, in addition to models with just one of the theories.

Isono (2024) also discusses its prediction for verb-final structures in languages like Japanese. Consider the following simple SOV sentence:(12) Kisya-ga giin-o koogekisita. reporter-nom senator-acc attacked ‘(The) reporter attacked (the) senator.’In a simple dependency-based processing, two dependencies are completed at the verb: one with the subject and another with the object. DLT therefore predicts a locality effect due to the length of these dependencies. For example, when the subject-verb distance is lengthened by an intervening element, as in (13), the verb should be harder to process than in (12).(13) a. Kisya-ga kizi-de giin-o koogekisita. reporter-nom article-in senator-acc attacked ‘(The) reporter attacked (the) senator in (the) article.’ b. Kisya-ga yotoo-no giin-o koogekisita. reporter-nom ruling.party-gen senator-acc attacked ‘(The) reporter attacked (the) senator of (the) ruling party.’A factor that must be controlled for to evaluate this prediction is the facilitatory effect of the intervening element. A matrix adverbial like kizi-de ‘in (the) article’ in (13a) can have a facilitatory effect on the verb in two ways: by reinforcing the activation of the predicted verb node (Vasishth & Lewis, 2006), and by making the verb more predictable (Hale, 2001; Konieczny, 2000; Levy, 2008). Such a facilitatory effect would cancel out the locality effect. A structure like (13b) is more suitable for the evaluation of the locality effect at the verb because the intervening element is a modifier on a matrix argument, and is therefore less likely to affect the activation or prediction of the verb. Isono and Hirose (2023) report that Japanese subject-verb dependencies still fail to show a locality effect even when structures like (13b) are used (also see Nakatani & Gibson, 2008, 2010). This result is problematic for DLT.

Notably, it is not the case that CLT predicts a null effect for all regions of a verb-final structure. For example, (15) is not fully incremental because the subject kisya-ga and the object modifier yotoo-no cannot be combined. This predicts a locality effect at the object head giin-o. Such locality effects between clausemates in Japanese are observed in self-paced reading experiments reported by Isono and Hirose (2023). See Figure 3 in the Experiment section for a visual illustration of the difference between the predictions of DLT and CLT for a verb-final structure. This is an example of the general divergence of DLT and CLT predictions in head-final structures: DLT predicts integration cost at the final head, while CLT predicts integration cost at dependents before the head.

One observation that still needs explanation is that Japanese clause-final verbs do show a locality effect when the argument is a wh-element (Ono & Nakatani, 2014) or an item requiring negative concord (Nakatani, 2023), rather than a simple nominative-marked NP. For example, -sika ‘only’ attaches to a noun phrase as a suffix and requires the predicate to be negated, as in (16). Using sentences like (16), Nakatani (2023) found that the matrix verb sinzi-nakat-ta ‘did not believe’ was more difficult to process when the sika-marked subject was distant from the verb. That is, a subject-verb locality effect was observed. No comparable effect was found when the subject was a usual nominative subject or marked with -dake ‘only’, which is semantically similar to -sika but does not require a negative predicate.(16) Tentyoo-sika [ueetoresu-ga zyoorenkyaku-o nagut-ta-to] sinzi-nakat-ta manager-only [waitress-nom regular.customer-acc hit-past-that believe-neg-past node because ‘Because nobody but (the) manager believed that (the) waitress hit (the) regular customer,…’Though CLT per se does not predict the contrast between sika-marked and ordinary subjects, it can be explained as an informational locality effect (Futrell, Gibson, & Levy, 2020; Hahn et al., 2022) under CCG-based parsing. The maximally incremental parse of (16) is the following (the internal structure of the complement clause is omitted):(17) We assume that a sika-marked subject is inherently type-raised to select a negated verb phrase, Sneg\NP. This means that the parser predicts a negated verb phrase when the sika-marked subject is encountered. This prediction would facilitate the processing of the negated verb downstream (Hale, 2001; Levy, 2008). However, this subject cannot be combined with the subsequent input until the complement clause is completed, as in a previous example (15). The subject expecting a negative verb phrase should then suffer from decay and/or interference while the complement clause is processed, and the precise information of the subject can be lost in some trials. If the neg feature on the subject is forgotten, the facilitatory effect at the verb would disappear. Since this forgetting is more likely to occur when the subject is held longer in memory, the loss of the facilitatory effect surfaces as a locality effect. This explanation is in line with the data reported by Nakatani (2023), where the locality effect seems to arise as a result of exceptionally fast reading time when the subject is sika-marked and adjacent to the verb, rather than a slowdown when the subject is sika-marked and distant from the verb.

We used the BCCWJ-SPR2 dataset (Asahara, 2022) to evaluate the prediction of CLT for naturalistic texts in Japanese and compare it with that of DLT. BCCWJ-SPR2 is a dataset of reading times collected online from native speakers of Japanese. The dataset uses texts of the Balanced Corpus of Contemporary Written Japanese (BCCWJ) (Maekawa et al., 2014). Reading times were collected using the non-cumulative, moving window self-paced reading method (Just et al., 1982). The texts were divided into bunsetsu, a group of morphemes that must be pronounced together (Hashimoto, 1934), and one bunsetsu was presented at a time. A bunsetsu is shown as a single orthographic word in the transcription used in this paper (i.e., bunsetsu boundaries are indicated by spaces). The participant pressed a key to proceed to the next word, and the time between one button press and the next was recorded as the reading time for that bunsetsu.

This study analyzes a subset of data from BCCWJ-SPR2 that uses the texts for which their Universal Dependencies (UD) annotations (de Marneffe et al., 2021; Nivre et al., 2020) are published (Asahara et al., 2018; Omura et al., 2021).4,5 By calculating both DLT and CLT costs from the same UD annotation, we ensure that the difference in the prediction of these theories is due to the theories, not due to any accidental differences in how the respective automated parsers for dependency and CCG resolve structural ambiguities. It also allows the same metric to be applied in DLT and CLT when measuring the distance of a string that intervenes in a non-local integration. We developed a simple pipeline Python script to calculate DLT and CLT costs from the UD annotation, which can be used in future studies to test the predictions of these theories for human behavioral or neural data associated with any linguistic resources with UD annotation. The materials in the subset all belong to the PB register of the corpus, which is a collection of texts taken from books of various genres. The materials consist of 83 samples, each of which is an excerpt from a book.

We randomly divided the 83 samples into 41 exploratory samples and 42 confirmatory samples of roughly the same text size. This is because there are multiple possible implementations of DLT and CLT, depending on how to measure the distance and what rules are assumed for CCG, as described below, and it is difficult to decide theoretically which implementations are the best. We first tested those multiple possible implementations against the exploratory samples, and the best-performing variant was submitted to the analysis with the confirmatory samples to ensure that the significant effects are not unique to the particular data. This way, we attempt a fair comparison of the core ideas of the two theories (Shain et al., 2022).

We also need to specify some implementational details of the theories. Specifically, both CLT and DLT need a distance metric, i.e., a way to quantify the non-locality of an integration; CLT also needs a specific rule set (see Table 2 for the full structure of the choices). These implementational details should be distinguished from the core idea of CLT and DLT that CCG- or dependency-based distance predicts locality effect (Isono, 2024). Since we want to test the core claims, and the best implementation depends on the data we are dealing with (described below), we search for the best implementation in the exploratory stage and then test its performance in the confirmatory stage.

The distance metric reflects the assumption about the amount of computational resources consumed to process the intervening element. It is essentially an approximation, and one way of counting that worked for one language may not necessarily be appropriate in another. For example, even if counting nouns and verbs may have worked for English, it may not work for Japanese, given that the nature of nouns and verbs differ between these languages. For this reason, we consider several possible distance metrics. We try different metrics not only for CLT but also for DLT for a fair comparison, although the original DLT (Gibson, 2000) is committed to a specific metric. Specifically, we consider the following three distance metrics:The number of nouns (with UD part-of-speech tags NOUN and PROPN) and verbs (VERB) (this version will be indicated with the suffix _nv); this is close to the original metric used by DLT (Gibson, 2000)The number of nouns, verbs, adjectives (ADJ) and adverbs (ADV) (suffix _nvjr); this is close to the metric used by the original version of CLT (Isono, 2024)The number of characters (suffix _char)
The number of nouns (with UD part-of-speech tags NOUN and PROPN) and verbs (VERB) (this version will be indicated with the suffix _nv); this is close to the original metric used by DLT (Gibson, 2000)
The number of nouns, verbs, adjectives (ADJ) and adverbs (ADV) (suffix _nvjr); this is close to the metric used by the original version of CLT (Isono, 2024)

The choice of CCG rule set similarly reflects the assumption about the level of incrementality, which may depend on factors such as the language, the difficulty of the secondary task, the population, etc. We consider the following rule sets:6>, <, >T, >B (suffix _B1)>, <, >T, >B, >B2 (suffix _B2)The first set contains the most basic rules that are needed to parse dependents on the same head (e.g., the subject and the object of a clause-final verb) incrementally, for which there is much psycholinguistic evidence (Kamide et al., 2003; Kamide & Mitchell, 1999). The second set extends it with the >B2 rule, which is a more “powerful” variant of >B that allows two arguments (instead of one) to be inherited to the output category:(18)

In addition to the predictors of theoretical interest described above, a number of control predictors are included in the regression models. The only grammar-based control predictor is integration count, defined below:Integration count (dlt/clt_cnt): the number of integrations (dependency completion in DLT; binary rule application in CLT) made at the region in question.Integration count is included in the model for the following consideration. Integration cost is defined as the sum of the distance of the integrations made at the region (this definition originates in DLT (Gibson, 2000) and CLT follows it). By definition, then, it should correlate with the integration count of that region. We would like to distinguish these two factors not just because they are conceptually distinct, but also because they may have effects in the opposite direction, canceling each other out, as described below.

Dependency-based integration count is known to have a negative effect on reading times (Asahara, 2022; Asahara et al., 2019; Isono, 2024). The putative reason for the negative effect is that it is a proxy for the predictability of the word (Konieczny, 2000; Konieczny & Döring, 2003; Vasishth & Lewis, 2006). Integration count of n at word w means that there are n words that have a dependency relation with w (either the head or a dependent of w). These words may be informative in predicting w. For example, the presence of eat in context makes an edible object noun more likely to appear. Since predictable words are processed more quickly, it is reasonable to expect that words with larger integration counts are read more quickly. Isono (2024) showed that controlling for this confound is important in evaluating DLT: whlie Dotlačil (2021) previously observed a negative effect of DLT integration cost (distance) in the Natural Stories corpus, Isono observed that when DLT integration count was also included in the model, the distance had no significant effect while the count had a significant negative effect.8

For the same reason, we speculated that CCG-based integration count has a negative effect on reading times and controlled for it in the statistical modeling. If the human parser compresses the syntactic information of the context into CCG constituents, as postulated by CLT, the number of CCG integrations that take place at a region reflects the amount of such information that is relevant for the current region. Unlike dependency-based integration count, there has not been clear evidence for the effect of CCG-based integration count. Several studies have investigated CCG node count, (Kajikawa et al., 2024; Ozaki et al., 2024; Stanojević et al., 2023), which differ from integration count in counting unary rules such as type-raising. We exclude unary rules from integration count since only binary rules, not unary rules, can increase integration cost (because unary rules are not integration of two elements) and can be correlated with predictability.

We also included several other non-grammatical control predictors in the regression model that are available for the current dataset and often included in corpus analysis (Demberg & Keller, 2008; Demberg et al., 2013; Dotlačil, 2021; Isono, 2024; Shain et al., 2016). They are listed below.The position of the sentence in the sample (SPR_sentence_ID). This is expected to have a negative effect on reading times since participants of reading experiments usually speed up towards the end of a coherent text and also through the course of a reading experiment.The position of the bunsetsu in the sentence (SPR_bunsetsu_ID). This is also expected to have a negative effect since participants often speed up towards the end of a sentence.The number of characters in the bunsetsu (nchar). This should have a positive effect since longer texts should take longer to read.

We also included two kinds of surprisal values listed below. According to the surprisal theory (Hale, 2001; Levy, 2008), a word is more difficult to process when it is less expected. This difficulty is quantified as the surprisal value −log P(w|C), where P(w|C) is the probability of the word w given the context C. The surprisal values are expected to have a positive effect on reading times.The sum of unigram surprisal of the morphemes comprising the bunsetsu (uni_surp). In analysis of corpus-based reading time data, it is commonplace to include the frequency of the word to the statistical model. Doing this for a Japanese corpus is not straightforward because a bunsetsu often consists of many morphemes, and observing the exact bunsetsu can be quite rare even if it consists of frequent morphemes. This study instead considers the morpheme-level rarity of the text by using the sum of unigram (i.e., decontextualized) surprisal of the morphemes comprising the bunsetsu. The probability of each morpheme is taken from the unigram frequency table of the NINJAL Web Japanese Corpus (Asahara et al., 2014)9.Surprisal values from GPT-2 (gpt_surp), a Transformer-based large language model (Radford et al., 2019). We used the smallest model of the Japanese GPT-2 (japanese-gpt2-xsmall) published by rinna Co., Ltd. (Sawada et al., 2024).10 Surprisal values from the smallest (“extra-small”) model showed a better fit to the current corpus data compared to those from the small- and medium-sized models. This is consistent with previous reports that smaller GPT models are better at capturing reading times (Oh & Schuler, 2023; Shain et al., 2024). The model does not directly give bunsetsu-by-bunsetsu surprisal values because it relies on tokenization defined by the sentencepiece tokenizer (Kudo & Richardson, 2018). To address the mismatch, the token-based surprisal values were evenly distributed to characters comprising the token, and then this by-character surprisal values were summed up to obtain the by-bunsetsu surprisal values.

Our goal is to test whether the predictors of memory cost provided by CLT and DLT explain a variance in reading times that is not explained by other known predictors. Toward this goal, we initially conducted a simple linear mixed-effects modeling, following some previous work analyzing naturalistic reading time datasets (Demberg & Keller, 2008; Dotlačil, 2021; Isono, 2024). However, we faced a number of problems, and switched to a different approach. Most importantly, we could not fully appreciate variations between participants, and that motivates the final analysis, described below. The initial analysis is reported in Appendix II for transparency, and will also be mentioned below since some of the problems motivated the final analysis.

In each of these stages, the following analysis was conducted (Figure 6). First, data points from each participant was separately modeled by eight linear models: the baseline model containing just the control predictors; the DLT models containing DLT integration cost, storage cost, or both; the CLT models containing CLT integration cost, storage cost, or both; and the DLT + CLT model containing all the four costs (see Table 3). The models additionally contain predictor values from the previous region to model the spillover effect (Mitchell, 1984).11 All the predictors were z-transformed for the stability of model fitting. The reading times were log-transformed. These models were evaluated by 10-fold cross validation as follows. For each participant, the data was randomly split to 10 folds of equal size. In each of the 10 iterations, one of these folds was held out and the models were fit to the remaining nine folds. The log likelihoods (LLs) assigned by the models to the held-out data indicate their predictive fit. Accordingly, the increase in LL (ΔLL) when a predictor or a set of predictors is added to the model indicate the predictive power of the predictor(s) (Wilcox et al., 2023). In the exploratory stage, we looked at ΔLLs of the CLT models and DLT models compared against the baseline model to identify the best-performing variants. In the confirmatory stage, we made several comparisons addressing the theoretical questions. For each comparison, we conducted a permutation test (Wilcox et al., 2023): we took the distribution of the by-bunsetsu ΔLLs averaged over participants, and assessed whether the mean of ΔLLs is significantly above zero (i.e., one model performs better than the other), by generating a distribution of hypothetical mean ΔLLs by randomly flipping the sign of ΔLLs (equivalent to permuting the label for the model assigning the LL value for each bunsetsu) and locating the observed mean in this distribution.

This approach is motivated by a number of considerations. First, it allows the data from each participant to be modeled separately to fully appreciate between-participant variations. Human readers can vary in how they respond to various linguistic features (King & Just, 1991; Nicenboim et al., 2016). A common approach to take such variations into account is to fit a linear mixed-effects model (Baayen et al., 2008) to the entire dataset, with random effects addressing between-participant variations. This approach is standard in controlled experiments and is in fact taken in some previous studies analyzing naturalistic reading time data (Demberg & Keller, 2008; Dotlačil, 2021; Isono, 2024). We also took this approach at first, but the full model failed to converge. By modeling each participant separately, we avoid convergence issues while acknowledging that participants may respond differently to the factors considered here. Second, we ask whether the predictor of interest improves predictive fit to held-out data, rather than whether its overall effect for the entire dataset is significantly away from zero. Evaluating the predictive fit avoids spurious effects due to overfitting. Note that when by-participant modeling and evaluation based on predictive fit are combined, a predictor can be judged to be a significant contributor even when it has effects in opposing directions (slowdown or speedup) depending on the participant, as long as the effect is consistent within each participant. We return to this point in the subsection named “Additional analysis I.”

paras.sec_title: Additional Analysis I: The Direction of the Effects.
paras.text: DLT and CLT integration counts show relatively clear negative effects. This is consistent with the view that integration count is confounded with predictability, which is the reason why we included them in the regression models. It is also consistent with previous observations (Asahara, 2022; Asahara et al., 2019; Isono, 2024).

paras.sec_title: Additional Analysis I: The Direction of the Effects.
paras.text: The effect of CLT integration cost is significantly positive, which is consistent with the view that it indexes the degree of degradation of CCG constituents and retrieving degraded constituents take time. The effect of DLT integration cost is significantly negative. A negative effect of DLT integration cost is also reported by Dotlačil (2021), but is inconsistent with the view that DLT integration cost is related to retrieval difficulty. Also, recall that DLT integration cost was not predictive according to the log-likelihood based test in the first place. A possible interpretation of these results is that DLT integration cost is confounded with some unidentified factor that has a negative effect on reading time, but the alignment is not close enough to give DLT integration cost a strong predictive power.

paras.sec_title: Additional Analysis I: The Direction of the Effects.
paras.text: The results with DLT and CLT storage costs are interesting since, although they showed a larger predictive power than integration costs, the direction of the effects is less clear. If anything, the trend is negative. The original motivation for the DLT storage cost (which CLT adopts) predicts a positive effect since storage of items in memory should use cognitive resources and thus slow down processing (Gibson, 2000). The robust predictive power suggests that the effect of storage cost is consistent within each participant—though the direction of the effect is not necessarily consistent across participants. This is reminiscent of the observation by Nicenboim et al. (2016) that readers with relatively low memory capacity can speed up in memory-demanding structures. While their explanation for the speedup is based on retrieval failure, it is possible to think of a mechanism in which high storage cost leads to speedup (Isono & Kajikawa, 2026). A high storage cost means that there is much linguistic information that has to be carried on to integrate with future input. Slowdown is necessary to process the intervening material correctly with the remaining resource. But an alternative strategy that a reader can take is to rush to get out of the demanding structure and avoid the risk of losing the stored information. This can sacrifice the understanding of the intervening element, but some readers may find it good enough (Ferreira et al., 2002). Given the possibility of such between-participant variability, we believe that the weakly negative direction of the DLT/CLT storage costs do not immediately undermine the hypothesis. Admittedly, there remains a possibility that what we see as the significant predictive power of DLT/CLT storage cost reflects something very different from storage cost. One possible way to be more confident in the cost-based interpretation would be to see the correlation between the direction of the effect and the cognitive capacity of each participant. If lower capacity readers tend to speed up and higher capacity readers tend to slow down, it would reinforce the cost-based interpretation. But we leave it for future study since the current dataset does not contain information about working memory capacity of participants.

In this study, we investigated whether memory effects during the reading of naturalistic texts in Japanese can be predicted by two contrasting syntax-based theories: DLT, based on dependency grammar, and CLT, based on Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG). These two theories share the idea that complicated syntactic structures can tax working memory, but have different assumptions regarding what structures are taxing. DLT assumes that long dependencies (e.g., subject-verb dependencies) are difficult. CLT assumes that processing difficulty arises from failure of information compression based on logical inference about sentence structure. Both theories posit that two mental mechanisms incur processing cost: integration of new input to the past context, and storage (or maintenance) of the past context. Previous studies show that DLT integration cost has difficulty predicting reading times based on English corpora (Demberg & Keller, 2008; Dotlačil, 2021), while CLT integration cost can (Isono, 2024). Less has been known about the corpus-level effect of storage cost on reading times (cf. Isono, 2024). By using a head-final language, Japanese, we put these theories to a further test. Testing DLT and CLT in a head-final language is important because they make contrastive predictions as to where memory-based processing difficulties arise.

paras.sec_title: Memory-Constrained CCG as a Candidate for the Universal Processing System
paras.text: Notably, some characteristics of the processing of head-final structures noted in the psycholinguistic literature fall out from these general assumptions. It has been observed that pre-head processing plays a key role in head-final structures (Kamide et al., 2003; Kamide & Mitchell, 1999; Nakatani, 2023; cf. Pritchett, 1992). Pre-head processing is predicted by CCG since the grammar itself is equipped with combinatory rules which allow arguments and adjuncts to be combined into single constituents before the head is seen. Furthermore, CLT correctly predicts that memory-based processing cost of a head-final structure is not concentrated on the head, as observed in previous experiments (Levy & Keller, 2013; Nakatani & Gibson, 2010; cf. Safavi et al., 2016). This CCG-based, universalist account contrasts with an alternative account of the lack of processing difficulty at clause-final verbs, according to which speakers of verb-final languages have a special strategy or capacity that allows them to process long dependencies without much difficulty (Levy & Keller, 2013; Nakatani & Gibson, 2010).

While the failure of DLT integration cost in the current study is in line with previous reports based on English corpora (Demberg & Keller, 2008; Dotlačil, 2021; Isono, 2024) and Japanese controlled experiments (Isono & Hirose, 2023; Nakatani & Gibson, 2010), it may appear puzzling or dubious given the straightforwardness of the idea that longer dependencies are more difficult to process. It should be emphasized that the current result does not deny that dependencies are relevant for processing. In some trivial sense, it is of course essential for comprehension to establish the relation between, for example, the head noun of a subject and the verb. It is probably the case that the verb triggers retrieval of the subject, as usually assumed. But that does not necessarily result in a locality effect, as predicted by DLT. If the subject is activated elsewhere before the verb is seen, for example, at the object (in an SOV language), the subject-verb locality effect would not arise at the verb. In other words, though dependency probably is important in comprehension, the parser can integrate words more eagerly than suggested by dependency-based processing. CLT pinpoints elements that are still difficult for the parser to integrate because of the complexity of the logical inference required.

Nor is the current result contradictory to the suggestion that grammars and productions of natural languages tend to minimize dependency length (Futrell, Levy, & Gibson, 2020; Temperley & Gildea, 2018). Dependency length minimization can be a result of storage cost minimization, since storing a prediction for a longer time results in a larger storage cost when the cost of the entire sentence is evaluated. And we did observe significant effect of DLT storage cost on reading times. Whether CLT (integration or storage) cost provide better or supplementary explanation for word order variations remains as a future topic.

With the current dataset, we observed that storage cost has a robust predictive power that is larger than that of (CLT) integration cost. This highlights the importance of storage cost in sentence processing, which is in fact a very old idea (Gibson, 2000; Just & Carpenter, 1992; Kimball, 1973; Lewis, 1996; Miller & Chomsky, 1963; Stabler, 1994; Yngve, 1960), though more recent, corpus-based reading times studies often exclusively focused on integration cost (Demberg & Keller, 2008; Dotlačil, 2021; Shain et al., 2016).

Memory limitations can affect parsing preferences as well as reading times. While the current study focuses on increase in reading times due to CLT costs, a possible extension is to explain parsing preference by avoidance of CLT costs, as Gibson (2000) did with DLT, and as suggested by a reviewer. With regard to Japanese, there is a line of study investigating the attachment ambiguity of arguments to verbs (Aoshima et al., 2004; Kamide & Mitchell, 1999; Miyamoto, 2002; Nakano et al., 2002; Omaki et al., 2014). Kamide and Mitchell (1999) investigated sentences like (19), in which the dative noun gakusei-ni ‘student-dat’ is ambiguous between the matrix clause and embedded clause readings.(19) Kyooju-ga [?gakusei-ni [?tosyokansisyo-ga kasita] mezurasii komonjo-o professor-nom student-dat librarian-nom lent unusual ancient.manuscript-acc miseta. showed ‘The professor showed (the student) the unusual ancient manuscript that the librarian had lent (the student).’Kamide and Mitchell observed that Japanese speakers prefer the matrix reading, and took that result as supporting the pre-head hypothesis that structural analysis of arguments begins before the head (verb) is observed.

In CLT, the preference can be explained by the difference in the storage cost between the matrix and embedded readings when the ambiguous dative noun gakusei-ni is read. The matrix reading is simply obtained by clustering the dative noun with the preceding nominative, as in (20a). The storage cost at the dative noun is 1. In contrast, the embedded reading requires the parser to refrain from clustering at this point, and combining the dative noun with the following embedded subject, as in (20b). Note that we assume that the dative noun and the embedded subject are combined by the >Dx rule (Hoyt & Baldridge, 2008) to generate the prediction for a verb with the usual argument structure, (T\NPnom)\NPdat. The storage cost at the dative noun will be 2 in this case. If a parser resolves temporal structural ambiguity by minimizing storage cost, the matrix reading should be preferred.(20)

This line of research, however, also reveals a constraint imposed on psycholinguistic research using CLT. Aoshima et al. (2004) studied a more complicated case of temporal ambiguity regarding the attachment of a fronted wh-phrase (note that Japanese wh-phrases are in situ by default). They found that readers associate the wh-phrase with the embedded verb. They suggest that their result is due to the parser’s preference to assign a thematic role to the wh-phrase as early as possible. The result, however, contrasts with the aforementioned result of Kamide and Mitchell (1999), who found the preference for the matrix attachment. Aoshima et al. note that two factors of their materials may be responsible for the disagreeing results: even the matrix reading involves scrambling, and the ambiguous noun is a wh-element. To implement this account in CLT, we first have to formulate a CCG analysis of (long-distance) scrambled wh-phrase in Japanese. Analysis of wh-elements in Japanese is complicated by the fact that the scope of the question is marked by a particle ka attached to the verb, not by the wh-phrase as in English. Establishing such an analysis requires a thorough discussion in the realm of theoretical linguistics and is beyond the scope of this paper (in the current corpus study, we tentatively ignored the distinction between wh- and non-wh-phrases). This is an instance of the general constraint in using CLT that we need a theoretical analysis of the target phenomenon in CCG. Obtaining such an analysis is more difficult than drawing a dependency graph to generate predictions in DLT, because CCG has a more rigorous view on syntax and its relation to semantics. This situation is frustrating, but we believe it is something that linguistics must go through: if competence grammar and performance are closely related (and they should; see below), we should seek an explanation that addresses both theoretical and psycholinguistic questions.

The current result shows that memory units defined by the limitation of the grammatical operations of CCG predict processing difficulty in real-time performance. This is in line with the strict competence hypothesis (SCH) (Steedman, 2000), according to which the parser does not build structure beyond what is defined by the competence grammar (Isono, 2024). SCH is the extreme version of the competence hypothesis, which assumes a close relationship between competence and performance (Ades & Steedman, 1982; Bresnan & Kaplan, 1982; Chomsky, 1965; Momma & Phillips, 2018; Phillips, 1996, 2012; Sag & Wasow, 2011). It should not be taken as collapsing the distinction between competence and performance, as competence-backed performance can still be limited by external factors such as memory limitations, attention, etc. Yet, SCH achieves a parsimonious account of human language faculty.

SCH can be understood by comparing CCG-based parsing with the left-corner parsing strategy. CCG-based parsing assumed here resembles arc-eager left-corner (AELC) parsing of a context-free grammar (CFG) (Resnik, 1992). For example, the CFG tree that an AELC parser would posit when the input is John attacked is as follows:(21) The analysis expressed by the tree is that the string John attacked will be an S if an NP follows. This is exactly what the CCG analysis expresses by assigning the category S/NP to the string. In fact, some studies using AELC parsing employ a CCG-like notation where a state like (21) is in fact expressed as S/NP (Rasmussen & Schuler, 2018; van Schijndel et al., 2013). AELC parsing has been popular in psycholinguistics since it correctly predicts the processing difficulty of center-embedded structures compared to left- and right-branching structures (Abney & Johnson, 1991). CCG-based (bottom-up) parsing provide an essentially same account, namely by the exceptionally large amount of memory space required. In CCG-based parsing (with canonical rules), there are three separate constituents when the parser reaches the depth of a doubly center-embedded structure:(22) ThereporterwhoNP/S/NPthesenatorwhoNP/S/NPJohnNP

Despite these similarities, CCG-based parsing complies with SCH, while left-corner parsing does not, and as a consequence, CCG-based parsing offers a simpler explanation of our incremental parsing ability (Isono, 2024). First, CCG-based parsing needs no special mechanism to handle displacement phenomena such as relativization since the grammar handles displacement and prediction with the same rules (B and T) that are used to model incrementality. Extending AELC to embrace displacement requires highly complicated extragrammatical structure building rules to ensure both incrementality and grammaticality, as seen in attempts to do that in Minimalist Grammars (Hunter, 2019; Stanojević & Stabler, 2018). Second, CCG-based parsing offers the semantics for the fragment for free, as it is defined in the grammar. This is crucial for a comprehension model because experimental facts show that the semantics of the fragment is available in real-time (Kamide et al., 2003; Tanenhaus et al., 1995). In AELC parsing, additional specification is needed for the semantics for the fragment.

There are two different notational conventions for functional categories. The one we adopt here, used in CCG, always places the resulting category to the left of the argument category. The other, used in type-logical variants (Lambek, 1958, 1961, i.a.) places the resulting category always on top of the argument category.

Steedman and colleagues have assumed that type-raising only takes place in the lexicon and applies only to certain categories (Steedman, 2026; Steedman & Baldridge, 2011). One reason for this is that type-raising of some categories, such as N and S\NP, overgenerates island-violating sentences. As Isono (2024) points out, however, such a restriction is too strong and undergenerates. This study follows Isono (2024) in assuming type-raising is a syntactic operation and some other factors, not necessarily syntactic, are responsible for the island phenomena (Chaves & Putnam, 2020; Kubota & Levine, 2020)

The dependency tree assumed here, based on Universal Dependencies, is different from that assumed in the original DLT paper (Gibson, 2000) in that there is no trace. This does not change the prediction that object relative clauses are costly at the embedded verb compared to subject relative clauses.

Two versions of UD annotation for BCCWJ are published depending on the granularity of the morphological analysis. We use the coarser version (the long unit word version; Omura et al., 2021) since DLT and CLT are mainly concerned with syntactic structures.

As a reviewer pointed out, another rule that is often used in CCG and could be included in the list is the forward crossed composition rule >Bx (Steedman, 2000). It can be used in Japanese when the order of the dependents does not follow the canonical order specified by the head (e.g., scrambling). If that line of analysis is employed, the CLT cost will increase (if we just employ the >Bx rule) compared to the canonical order, or stay the same (if we also employ another rule that enables incremental processing of scrambled word order). In this study, we adopt a simplifying assumption that all the observed word orders are canonical and avoid using the >Bx rule. This means that we focus on the costs due to where the dependents are placed relative to each other, but not the potential cost of scrambling.

The sentence ID given in the UD annotation is PB32_00008-50; the final verb cluster kaki-okut-ta-nodeat-ta ‘write-send-past-emphasis-past’ is simplified for the reason of space. The most incremental CCG tree (without the >B2 rule) for the sentence is as follows:(i) The $ symbol in the category of ni ‘to’ indicates an arbitrary number of arguments. See Steedman (2000) for the definition of the symbol, and Bekki (2010) for the use of the symbol for the analysis of Japanese adverbials.

As a reviewer points out, GPT surprisal already exists as a powerful metric of predictability. Isono (2024) found, however, that dependency-based integration count is significant even when GPT surprisal is included in the regression model. This is possibly because human prediction relies more on structured representation of recent context, while GPT has access to much longer context (for a related observation, see Kuribayashi et al., 2022). For this reason, the current analysis also includes both integration count and GPT surprisal.
